p.seg: To accept five thousand Wú (吳) courtesans
, is the same as the errors of Hào (晧).
The enfeoffment of women
, brought chaos to the Six States;
like posthumously bestowing a title on one's maternal great-grandmother
, it violates the ancient Way.
All these improper matters
, are recorded in the previous book
, and indeed they tarnish his brilliant plans.
The historian dares not conceal them.
○ *Yù Lǎn* (御覽) 96.
"Biàn Zōng Lùn" (辨宗論)
"Biàn Zōng Lùn" (辨宗論)
The various Daoist priests who traveled with me
, all studied the Way of the mind and spirit
, seeking understanding beyond words.
I, resting my head due to illness and having little to do
, have quite a few leisure days
, so I will briefly express the meaning of the origin
, hoping to settle the understanding of seeking the source.
The theory of the Buddhists
is that, although the Way of the Sage is distant
, accumulated learning can reach it
; when accumulation is exhausted, wisdom arises
, it should not be gradual enlightenment.
The theory of the Confucians
The Sacred Way is profound and subtle;
though close to Yán Hui's sagacity,
it cannot be fully comprehended in its entirety,
and its principles ultimately converge to a single extreme.
There is a Daoist with a new discourse who believes:
That stillness and illumination are subtle and profound,
not admitting of stages;
that accumulated learning is boundless,
so why cut oneself off?
Now, we discard the gradual enlightenment of the Śākyas,
and take their ability to attain the goal;
we discard the approximate understanding of the Confucians,
and take their ultimate unity.
Ultimate unity is different from gradual enlightenment,
and the ability to attain is not approximate understanding.
Therefore, though the principles they reject
are in agreement with what we each take,
they are far removed from both Confucius and the Śākyas.
I consider the words of the two discourses on saving beings,
the tenets of the Daoists,
and the doctrines of those who have attained understanding,
and dare to presume to offer a compromise.
I humbly consider this new discourse to be true.
I merely respond to your question,
hoping for eventual enlightenment.
○ The following is also in the eighteenth volume of the "Guǎng Hóngmíng Jí."
<Reply to Fǎ Xù's Questions>
Fǎ Xù asked:
"Having respectfully read your insightful discussion,
although clarifying the ultimate principle is subtle,
a single awakening brings complete understanding.
While I rejoice in the newly revealed explanation,
I still have some doubts.
Clear-sighted individuals use understanding of principle to sever desires,
while the complacent become entangled in burdens due to delusion.
Severing desires originates from seeing the principle,
while entanglement arises from deviating from the source.
Why do I say this?
The sutra says that new learners who are separated from prajna (wisdom)
are like the blind without a guide.
Thus, embracing principle eradicates suffering,
which is clearly demonstrated here.
If one's pursuit has not yet gradually approached the great source,
and aspirations are still burdened by worldly defilements,
then endless eons of toil
will lead to a distant and uncertain fruition.
Since I harbor doubts,
I humbly await your esteemed instruction."
The first reply:
"The path is contrary to the mundane,
principle is unrelated to the worldly,
therefore expedient means are used to make them accessible.
Although expedient means are provisional,
their purpose lies in the non-provisional.
Although wisdom is genuine,
its ability can be unreal.
The unreal does not harm the genuine;
its essence lies in benefiting beings.
The unreal does not follow falsity;
benefiting beings leads back to the essence.
Such a calamity,
is a futile effort,
hoping for a result like the shining sun.
Xù asked again:
According to the argument,
the Dao of Confucius and Buddhism are the same,
saving beings from falsity,
also should not be different.
But the realm of the divine,
even if wise,
is what Confucius did not teach;
the subtlety of true reality,
even if foolish,
is what the Shakya clan (Buddhists) must teach.
Then, the teachings of the two sages,
why are they so contradictory?
I answered again:
The difference between the two teachings
lies in adapting to the region and responding to things,
the land where they are transformed is different.
To greatly examine them,
the Huá Mín (華民, Chinese people) are quick to grasp principles,
but slow to accept instruction.
Therefore, close off their accumulated learning
and open up their understanding of the ultimate principle.
The Yí Rén (夷人, foreign people) are quick to accept instruction,
but slow to grasp principles.
Therefore, close off their sudden understanding
and open up their gradual enlightenment.
Although gradual enlightenment can be achieved,
they are ignorant of the reality of sudden understanding.
Although the ultimate principle is known to be relied upon,
the hope of accumulated learning is cut off.
This is because the Huá Rén (華人, Chinese people) understand principles without gradualism,
and dismiss the Dao as needing no learning.
The Yí Rén (夷人, foreign people) understand principles through learning,
and dismiss the Dao as being gradual.
Therefore, although expediency and reality are the same,
their application differs.
In the past, Xiàng Zǐqī (向子期) considered Confucianism and Daoism to be one,
Yīng Jífǔ (應吉甫) said that Confucius and Laozi could be equated,
all wanting to perceive the source,
how much more so those who have attained the truth!
Xù (勖) asked three times:
Zhòng (重) replied,
that because Huá (華, Chinese) and Yí (夷, foreign) people have natures that make things difficult or easy,
the two sages (Confucius and Laozi) dispensed different and similar teachings.
Zhòng Fāng's adherence to custom
can be considered beautiful!
However, if the profoundly clear sees
and sets an example from above,
the foolish and ignorant people,
submit and follow from below.
Therefore, setting an example should carefully consider the policies,
and submission must affirm its principles.
If you command to abandon the path of Confucian sage-learning,
and释 (Shì, Buddhism) open a gradual enlightenment path,
with traps and footprints already in confusion,
how can the common people return to the truth?
Third Response:
Winter and summer have different natures,
relying on spring and autumn as the beginning and end;
day and night have distinct uses,
depending on morning and evening for recurrence.
Moreover, how can the principle of utmost refinement
be directly connected to people of utmost coarseness?
Therefore, following gradual enlightenment
is how to secretly create sudden understanding;
relying on Confucian teachings
is how to silently achieve sage-learning.
Sage-learning does not go beyond the Six Classics,
and is attained through the Six Classics;
sudden understanding is not found in the Three Treasures (Tripiṭaka),
but is the fruit of the Three Treasures.
The traps and footprints are clear,
why doubt their confusion!
Once the fish and rabbit are caught,
the common people are saved.
<Reply to Monk Wéi's Question>
Now, if one speaks highly of a worthy person,
one still acknowledges their worthiness.
If one speaks highly of a sage,
how can one then turn around and say they are not a sage?
What people use daily without understanding
is the ignorance of the common people,
while only the Buddha fully comprehends the sublimity of true reality.
Now, to take this sublime reality
and expect the ignorant to understand it,
is something that has never happened.
If something is not understood,
how can one not believe in clear and straightforward explanations?
Since you acknowledge the teachings of Śākya to be correct,
why do you consider the teachings of Confucius to be wrong?
<Reply to Fǎ Gāng's Questions>
Zhú Fǎgāng asks:
Respectfully examining your insightful discourse,
I have deeply studied its ultimate principles,
subtly judging between the provisional and the real,
preserving the essence of Confucianism and Daoism,
and the legacy of the teachings of Confucius and Śākya.
Your straightforward arguments offer a compromise,
a truly novel perspective,
which can be described as diverting the flow to its source,
and illuminating and fully expressing it.
However, in your detailed replies to Xù and Wéi,
some say that you use expedience to achieve understanding,
It is learning, but not enlightenment.
Your setting up of abstruse phrases is in vain,
having nothing to do with inner feelings,
is what I secretly find unsettling.
How do I say this?
The way is separated by heaven,
and approaches the double precipice of danger.
If learning does not gradually lead to its source,
there will not even be a faint resemblance.
If galloping has a boundary,
and thought does not go beyond its position,
how can one ascend the divine cliff?
From where can one surpass the peak of opportunity?
If one diligently works on the existent
while sitting and contemplating on the nonexistent,
it is like wielding a brush following the rules of Zhōng Zhāng,
achieving the skill of Yì and Yǎng.
It would clearly not be possible!
For even the same type of existent is not a great impediment,
yet one still cannot master this and excel at that.
How much more so when the existent and nonexistent are utterly opposed,
can they instead become mutually connected?
It is also said:
"When the encumbrances are not yet exhausted,
nothing cannot be attained.
Only when the disadvantages of encumbrances are exhausted,
can non-being be attained."
The discourse says:
Now, the great Dao that penetrates to the marrow and vital regions,
the mysterious path that destroys the axle of the chariot,
nothing is more harmful than the accumulation of possessions.
For having cannot dispel having,
and he who dispels having must have nothing;
one cannot first exhaust the burdens of having,
and then attain nothingness.
As you say,
when the burdens are exhausted, there is nothing;
but for the burdens to disappear on their own,
it truly requires waiting,
it truly requires waiting,
therefore one cannot but have nothing,
hence nothingness is prized.
Like a heavy darkness that disperses on its own,
without the need for fire or sun;
without the need for fire or sun,
then one cannot but establish it,
thus illuminating nothingness as supreme.
To drop levels and value sudden enlightenment,
you will likely stumble here!
In moments of leisure,
I hope you will consider my humble explanation.
The reply says:
Your question states:
"Even if they have similarities, they are still obstacles,
it is still not possible to enjoy this and be good at that,
how much more so with existence and non-existence which are completely opposite,
yet can they somehow communicate with each other?"
This doubt arises from being constrained by what you are accustomed to.
Now, one who specializes in playing with brush and paper,
may well not be skilled in bow and arrow;
once skilled in bow and arrow,
